name: Tomas Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for a side. Everything here is confidential. What did you work on before lunch?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Tomas Weber, forty-three, and I lead the transport accounts team at an accounting firm that prepares accounts and tax returns. I matched a depot's fuel cards to its ledger this morning and caught a week entered twice; I like giving the owner a clear answer before tax is due. I dislike deadlines announced without asking who can actually review the files. I'm among our best reviewers, with a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else shapes your working week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I never use AI tools; I prefer to see a reliable error record before changing our checks. My wife Claire works at a community pharmacy, our children are six and ten, and we have a mortgage with about three months of expenses saved. My pay is typical for this senior job and there are some similar firms nearby. I tend to judge a change by what it costs and what it fixes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tax files would still arrive each week. A receipt scanner may save our juniors a little copying, but I would still reconcile the haulage clients' fuel bills against their books.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep checking the source documents before signing anything. I'd tell clients the firm remains responsible for their returns, whatever software sorted the receipts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage is ordinary for a senior accountant and our family has about three months of expenses saved. I don't use AI tools and I would be glad not to be pushed into another system. Our mortgage is manageable while my wife Claire and I both keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd continue leading the tax return review rota and reconcile the fuel ledgers by hand. I'd ask the partners to show us the scanner's error log at our January meeting, but I would not change my process without evidence. If the work and pay stay steady, we'd keep the same monthly mortgage payment and household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. I like a day where the figures and the job still make sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of today felt useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A depot manager brought me a stack of fuel cards with dates in the wrong week. I enjoyed finding the mismatch before it reached his tax return. I get tired of a partner calling every ordinary deadline an emergency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust the scanner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the scanner's error log checked against original fuel receipts, including missed duplicates. There are some other accounting firms nearby, so this job is not our only possible pay packet. I'd still rather solve the scanner question here than jump for no reason.

say: I would keep **source checks** on every tax return we sign.
I would keep the **firm responsible** for a client’s figures.
think: Our **three-month reserve** gives the family some room.
I prefer **known controls** while pay and work remain steady.
do: Continue **fuel-ledger reviews**, tax sign-off and our present mortgage budget.
Ask for the **scanner error log** at January’s meeting.
feel: I feel **calm** about our present work and money.
S0.quote: I like a day where the figures and the job still make sense.
fieldNote: His **typical senior pay**, three months saved and some nearby firms support a calm plateau.
His **scanner request** seeks evidence before changing familiar controls; he has never used AI tools.

steps.text: Continue tax reviews, fuel reconciliations and the same household budget
Ask partners for scanner error log at January meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Routine letters and first-pass checks could go to software, so fewer review days may be paid. I would want the partners to say whether my own Thursday client day stays on the rota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the proposed staffing numbers beside the error rate. I'd say a driver or depot owner still deserves an accountant who answers a question without sending another template.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my Thursday day disappears, we would lose part of my pay. Three months saved gives us search time, but Claire's pharmacy wage alone would not pay the mortgage and both children's costs. I am good at reviewing difficult transport returns, but I don't use AI and would need a careful demonstration before relying on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the partners for a written rota and three months of client correction counts. I'd keep the current paid Thursday calls while they exist. If they cut my day, I'd apply for a posted senior accounts opening at the local freight cooperative only after written mortgage-covering pay, a fixed start and school pickup hours are clear; otherwise I'd remain on my paid rota and keep checking openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about a possible wage cut. I can handle a changed worksheet better than a missing Thursday payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who collects your youngest on Thursdays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I collect our six-year-old from school on Thursday because Claire works the late pharmacy shift. A freight office that closes at six would need a confirmed club place and a wage that covers it. I would price that before accepting a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers would you ask the partners for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The correction count tells us whether the proposed review time is safe. If the partners will not give us the numbers, I can ask again in writing and keep my current checks. Some local firms hire, but a vacancy has to be advertised and paid.

say: I would ask for a **written rota** and correction counts.
I would protect a **client call** where a real answer is needed.
think: My **Thursday wage** could shrink if review days are cut.
Claire’s **pharmacy pay** cannot carry our mortgage alone.
do: Request the **written rota** and three-month correction count.
Keep **paid Thursday calls** while they remain available.
After **day cuts**, apply only for posted work with written mortgage pay, start and pickup.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost pay.
S1.quote: I can handle a changed worksheet better than a missing Thursday payslip.
fieldNote: A **possible own-day cut** drives the mood; three months saved provide time, not income replacement.
The **freight job** requires an advertised funded vacancy, written mortgage pay, fixed start and covered Thursday pickup.

steps.text: Request written rota and correction counts while keeping paid client calls
Apply after cut only for funded freight job with written mortgage pay, start and pickup

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could prepare and check the returns that fill most of my week. Robots around 2031 are later, but the accounting firm needs no robot to stop paying for desk reviews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for notice and an honest list of posts they can still fund. I'd tell our family we are protecting the mortgage before any holiday plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my senior review post could end in the first year after 2028. Three months of savings is helpful, but it is not a year of wages; Claire's pharmacy income would not cover our mortgage. Having a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification does not make this desk immune.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel the spring holiday booking costing five hundred before its deposit is due and hold that money for bills. I'd stay employed and watch posted finance vacancies at the freight cooperative. If the firm ends my post in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, I'd claim temporary income support and take a funded opening only with written mortgage-covering pay, a start date and Thursday pickup covered; without one, I'd keep any paid accounts work the firm still offers and continue looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Three months of savings is a useful pause, not a new salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Claire work more hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire and I would tell the children the holiday can wait and their school week stays the same. She could ask for an extra pharmacy shift, but we would count only a confirmed shift with someone covering pickup. I would put the mortgage due date on the kitchen calendar before calling anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a friend at the cooperative help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A friend at the freight cooperative is not a vacancy. I would check the posted role, pay and start in writing before moving. If no role exists, I would keep the firm's paid files and ask for income support as soon as the post ends.

say: I would ask for **honest notice** and funded posts.
I would put the **mortgage first** when telling our family.
think: My **review post** could end in the first year after AGI arrives in 2028.
Our **three-month reserve** cannot replace a year of wages.
do: Cancel the **one-off holiday booking** and hold five hundred for bills.
Watch **posted co-op finance vacancies** while employed; after 2028 post loss claim support and seek funded work.
Keep **paid files if offered** until written mortgage pay, start and pickup are secured.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected post loss.
S2.quote: Three months of savings is a useful pause, not a new salary.
fieldNote: **Thinking AI** reaches his desk work by 2028; 2031 robots provide no delay for the accounting post.
His **freight alternative** needs a posted funded vacancy, written mortgage pay, a start and pickup; paid files continue if unavailable.

steps.text: Cancel one-off spring holiday booking and reserve five hundred for bills
Claim temporary income support after 2028 post loss
Check posted funded co-op vacancies now; move after loss with written mortgage pay, start, pickup
Keep any paid accounts files offered if no funded vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would let me ask which client questions the firm can still charge to answer. AGI in 2031 would take much of our accounts and tax preparation; robots around 2034 don't extend my desk deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners to price the transport tax clinics before announcing them as my new job. I'd tell clients what a half-hour meeting costs rather than adding it silently to the return fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A depot owner may value a person who understands a disputed fuel claim, but a machine might explain it cheaply too. I would trust signed bookings more than my guess. Our three-month reserve should stay for the family, not fund unpaid evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd ask the partner for paid time to offer two transport clients a priced tax-clinic meeting. I'd run it only if both sign fees that cover the hours; if the partner refuses, I'd keep paid return work and leave the proposal on the table. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if tax work ends, I'd keep signed paid meetings or take a posted funded freight finance role only with written mortgage pay, start and pickup; while applying, I'd keep signed contracted meetings and any paid firm hours still offered; if neither job nor meetings exists, I'd claim income support if eligible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with time to test a real client fee. A client saying thank you is not a signed meeting fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the depot owner need explained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One depot owner asked whether a disputed fuel charge would change his tax bill. I enjoyed tracing it to the card receipt while he was there, and he left understanding the answer. I would ask whether he would pay for a scheduled meeting like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the firm will not fund the meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partner owns the client relationship, so I will not sell it privately after hours. If no paid time or two signed fees appear, the clinic remains an idea, and I continue with my salary. After 2031 a closed freight vacancy means I keep any paid firm work offered and search again.

say: I would propose **priced tax clinics** before calling them jobs.
I would tell clients the **meeting fee** in advance.
think: A **signed booking** matters more than a client’s interest in a meeting.
Our **reserve** cannot subsidise unpaid client evenings.
do: Offer **two priced clinics** only with paid time and signed covering fees.
Keep **signed contracted meetings** and any offered paid firm hours throughout the post-2031 application search.
After **2031 tax loss**, seek funded freight work with written mortgage pay, start and pickup; claim eligible support if nothing pays.
feel: I feel **anxious** until demand is signed.
S3.quote: A client saying thank you is not a signed meeting fee.
fieldNote: The **tax-clinic pilot** requires partner-paid time and two signed fees covering hours; refusal leaves him on paid returns.
The **2031 job path** needs a posted vacancy, written mortgage pay, start and pickup; support and paid work bridge failure.

steps.text: Offer two priced clinics only with partner-paid time and signed covering fees
Keep signed paid meetings and offered firm hours during applications
Take posted funded freight role after 2031 loss only with written mortgage pay, start and pickup
Claim eligible income support after loss if no paid meetings or vacancy exists

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade would let our children get older and let us bring the reserve from three months toward six. AGI in 2036 still reaches accounts and tax returns before robots arrive around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the firm to give us a long notice period and show what client services it will actually fund. I'd tell colleagues that a calendar helps only if wages keep arriving during the years on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be fifty-three when the tax desk changes, and I would still have a mortgage. Our youngest would be sixteen, while the older child would be twenty, but I would not put either child's wages into our plan. Six months saved would help us search, not retire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next January I'd transfer one hundred a month from our current budget into the reserve while both wages remain intact; if pay falls, I'd stop the transfer before missing a mortgage payment. I'd keep the paid review rota and ask for a written notice plan at the annual staff meeting. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if the tax post ends, I'd take only a posted funded finance role with written mortgage pay, start and pickup covered; if none fits, I'd claim income support and keep any paid firm hours still offered while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a future wage loss, but ten years lets us build more room. Six months of savings is search time, not retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would older children contribute in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Claire and I already know which standing order moves on payday. One hundred is possible while both of us keep our present wages, and we can check that each quarter. I would rather build that reserve than rely on our older child staying at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful notice plan contain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a notice plan with dates and named paid roles, not a speech. If the firm will not publish one, I keep the paid review rota while it is offered and check cooperative vacancies each quarter. I will not resign without a written start and salary.

say: I would request **dated notice** and funded client work.
I would tell colleagues **wages matter** during a long runway.
think: My **tax desk** remains exposed when AGI arrives in 2036, regardless of robots.
Six **months saved** would buy search time, not retirement.
do: Transfer **one hundred monthly** while both wages stay intact.
Seek a **written notice plan**; if refused, keep offered paid reviews and check cooperative vacancies quarterly.
After **2036 tax loss**, take funded work with written wage, start and pickup; otherwise claim support and keep offered paid hours.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about eventual wage risk despite current stability.
S4.quote: Six months of savings is search time, not retirement money.
fieldNote: His **current three-month reserve** could grow through a conditional monthly transfer, stopping if pay falls.
The **2036 exit** requires a posted funded vacancy, written mortgage pay, start and pickup; support and paid firm hours bridge gaps.

steps.text: Transfer one hundred monthly while both household wages remain intact
Ask for notice plan; if refused keep offered paid reviews and check co-op vacancies quarterly
Take posted funded finance role after 2036 loss only with written mortgage pay, start and pickup
Claim support and keep offered paid firm hours if no funded role

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my account reviews are desk work and the firm could end my wage quickly. Three months saved would help us search, but not pay the mortgage for a year. Written notice, temporary income support and a funded vacancy with real pay and a start date would help. A funded post is more useful than a comforting speech.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what happens to the client who gets a correct return but cannot explain a disputed fuel figure. I enjoy settling that question. I would only call it a future job if someone pays for the meeting.

headlineQuote: A funded post is more useful than a comforting speech.
portrait: At **forty-three**, Tomas leads transport accounts and tax-return reviews.
His **master’s** and chartered qualification support top skill and typical senior pay.
He **never uses AI**, preferring an error record before changing established checks.
Claire’s **pharmacy wage**, two schoolchildren, mortgage and three-month reserve shape his search limits.
Some **nearby firms** offer options, but a move needs written pay, start and pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his desk wage before the reserve covers a long search.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, temporary support and a funded post with real pay and start.
